title: What are insurers and agencies actually using AI for?
description: Where AI pays first for carriers, MGAs and agencies: ranked jobs, tool prices, the state AI rules, who signs off, and our job-ad count.
verdict: AI mostly assists people.[^1] Of 193 auto insurers in 2022, 96 used it to inform adjusters, none to deny claims.[^3]
Start with submission intake at carriers and policy checking at agencies.[^6] Underwriters spend up to 40% of time on admin.[^4]
Nearly half of agencies use AI, yet only 8% have it in daily workflows and 55% have no written policy.[^6][^7]
Thirty jurisdictions adopted the state regulators' AI bulletin; Colorado and New York wrote their own.[^8] You answer for vendor AI.[^10]
Keep a named person on every claim denial. Lawsuits alleging algorithms, not reviewers, drove health insurers' denials partly survived dismissal.[^12][^13]

headings.ranked: Where does AI pay first in insurance?
headings.buy-or-build: Should you buy AI tools or build your own?

summary: AI in insurance mostly reads and drafts: it pulls facts from submissions, claim files and policy forms so underwriters, adjusters and agents decide faster.[^4][^1][^2] The decision stays with your people: state regulators apply the same standards whatever the tool.[^15][^11] Clean submission data and real human checks make or break it.[^5][^12]
humanRole: Underwriters keep accept, decline and price. New York expects each adverse decision to state the information used and its source.[^10][^16]
Adjusters keep every claim denial. In the regulators' auto survey, 9 of 193 insurers used AI for claim approvals and none for denials.[^3]
A licensed producer checks anything a client sees. Treat AI output as a draft and verify limits, deductibles, exclusions and endorsements against the policy forms.[^17]

Senior management and the board own the AI program, with a cross-functional group such as underwriting, claims, compliance and legal.[^15][^11][^9] The bulletin lists checking AI output against expert review as one way to validate it.[^11]

ranked.name: Submission intake and triage (carriers and MGAs)
ranked.why: Underwriters spend up to 40% of their time on admin, and 51% of AI users say saving admin time is its main gain so far.[^4][^5] Only 10% of underwriting teams pre-sort broker email with AI today; 75% expect to within three years.[^18]
ranked.payoff: Hours from submission received to quote, and the share of submissions quoted.

ranked.name: Claim file summaries for adjusters (carriers)
ranked.why: Claims is the top AI area for auto insurers, and the main use is informing adjusters.[^3][^19] In a McKinsey case study, Aviva runs 80+ claims models and assesses complex liability 23 days faster.[^20]
ranked.payoff: Adjuster minutes per file review, and days to first offer.

ranked.name: Policy checking and quote comparison (agencies)
ranked.why: Coverage form analysis is agencies' second most common AI use, at 43%.[^6] Published tools start at $99 a month for 200 checks or comparisons a year.[^21]
ranked.payoff: Minutes per policy check, and errors caught before the client sees the policy.

ranked.name: Prospect and declarations-page intake (agencies)
ranked.why: Tools that pull a prospect's current policy and declarations page (the policy summary sheet) publish prices from $79 to $500 a month.[^22][^23] Routine data entry is one of agents' top four time-saving AI uses.[^24]
ranked.payoff: Minutes to start a quote, and quotes per producer per week.

ranked.name: Service email, renewal prep and meeting notes (agencies)
ranked.why: Agents who use AI say it saves them about 4 hours a week.[^24] Meeting notes (44%) and marketing content (43%) are their top time-saving uses.[^24]
ranked.payoff: Service hours per policy, and renewals prepared on time.

ranked.name: Fraud screening (carriers)
ranked.why: Fraud costs US consumers $308.6 billion a year, a coalition figure the NAIC cites.[^25] Among insurers the regulators surveyed, 58% in auto and 55% in home use or plan AI for it.[^19]
ranked.payoff: Hit rate of referrals to your special investigations unit, checked by customer group.

ownData.title: What are your peers hiring for?
ownData.intro: We counted US insurance job ads posted in the 30 days to 26 November 2026, by job title, in one job-ad database.[^26] An ad counts as mentioning AI if it names artificial intelligence, generative AI, ChatGPT, Copilot, AI tools, AI-powered or machine learning.[^26] AI shows up in modeling jobs far more than in the front-line jobs where the admin piles up.[^26][^4]

tables.title: What do insurers use AI for, by line of business?
tables.intro: From the NAIC's surveys of larger insurers, summarised in its own journal.[^19][^2] Surveys covered insurers with $250M+ in premium or a large state market share.[^32] Auto and home left out simpler statistical models and health counted them, so compare lines with care.[^19][^32]

rules.name: NAIC Model Bulletin on insurers' use of AI
rules.status: In force in 30 jurisdictions (NAIC map, 13 Nov 2026)
rules.what: You need a written AI program covering governance, risk controls and audit, scaled to the possible harm to consumers.[^15][^11] It covers vendor AI, and examiners can ask for your AI inventory, vendor contracts and testing.[^11] Recent adopters include Texas, South Carolina and North Dakota; check your state's version.[^8][^33]

rules.name: Colorado SB21-169 and Regulation 10-1-1
rules.status: In force: life since Nov 2023; auto and health since 15 Oct 2025
rules.what: Life, private auto and health insurers need a board-overseen framework for outside consumer data and the models that use it.[^9][^34] Commercial-only carriers and agencies are outside its scope today.[^9] Bias-testing reports are waived until the Division adopts testing rules for each line.[^35]

rules.name: New York Department of Financial Services (DFS) Circular Letter No. 7
rules.what: New York insurers must show that AI and outside data in underwriting and pricing don't discriminate unfairly, with the board responsible.[^10] You stay responsible for vendor tools, so contracts should give audit rights.[^10] Adverse-decision notices should name the information used and its source.[^16]

rules.name: California Insurance Bulletin 2022-5
rules.what: California's own guidance on bias in AI and big data; the NAIC lists it in place of the model bulletin.[^8]

rules.name: NAIC third-party data and model vendor framework
rules.what: It proposes a multi-state registry and yearly attestation for vendors of property and casualty (P&C) pricing and underwriting data and models.[^36][^37] Insurers would still own their own compliance.[^38]

watchOuts: Rubber-stamp review: a lawsuit alleges Cigna doctors denied over 300,000 payment requests at about 1.2 seconds each, and a court let it proceed.[^12][^14] Nothing is proven yet; still, log review time, sample decisions and show reviewers the evidence, not only the score.

Unequal outcomes: Black homeowners allege State Farm's claim-screening algorithms slowed and questioned their claims more; the claim survived dismissal in 2023.[^39] Test outcomes by group before and after go-live; Colorado and New York expect it for covered lines.[^9][^10]
Vendor AI treated as someone else's problem. The NAIC bulletin and New York keep you responsible for vendor models, so put audit rights and regulator cooperation in the contract.[^11][^10]

Client data pasted into public chatbots: 45% of agencies use public AI chatbots, and 55% have no written AI policy.[^7] Write a one-page policy, use a business account, and keep loss runs (claims histories) out of unapproved tools.[^17]
Trusting '95% accurate' extraction: one agent noted the last 5% 'is exactly where the E&O risk lives'.[^40] Check key fields against the source form and have a producer sign off.[^17]

Pilots that never reach the desk: 65% of agents used AI last year, but only 14% of agencies have rolled out a tool.[^24][^41] Pilot one workflow on one team with one owner and one measure; only about 5% of task-specific AI tools reach production with measurable return.[^42]

faq.q: How is AI used in insurance?
faq.a: Mostly to read and draft for the people who decide.[^1][^2] In regulators' surveys, claims and fraud lead in auto and home, and underwriting leads in life.[^19] Agencies use it most for marketing copy, coverage form analysis and contract review.[^6]

faq.q: Will AI replace insurance agents or underwriters?
faq.a: Nothing in the data points that way. Agents who use AI say it saves them about 4 hours a week.[^24] Regulators hold insurers to the same standards whatever tool helped make a decision.[^15][^11]

faq.q: What AI tools do insurance agents actually use?
faq.a: Mostly general chatbots: 45% of agencies use ChatGPT or similar public tools, 20% policy comparison tools and 13% data-extraction tools.[^7] Check what your agency management system already includes before you buy another tool.[^43]

faq.q: Is it safe to put client information into ChatGPT?
faq.a: Not in a free consumer account. Use an approved business tool, keep loss runs and financials out of unapproved platforms, and write a policy.[^17] 55% of agencies still have none.[^7]

faq.q: Which AI rules apply to insurers in my state?
faq.a: Thirty jurisdictions have issued the NAIC AI bulletin, per its 13 Nov 2026 map.[^8][^33] California, Colorado and New York have their own guidance or rules.[^8] Check your state's own text, because versions differ.[^33]

faq.q: How much do AI tools for insurance agencies cost?
faq.a: Published agency prices run from about $79 to $500 a month, checked 26 Nov 2026.[^21][^22][^23][^27] Most carrier underwriting and claims platforms publish no price.[^29][^30]

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy when the job is standard, such as policy checking, declarations-page intake or call answering, and you have no data team.[^44] Most enterprise AI is now bought: 76% of use cases, up from 53% in 2024.[^44] MIT found vendor partnerships reached production about twice as often as internal builds.[^42][^45]
buyVsBuild.build: Build when your guidelines, appetite and loss history are your edge, or you must explain every step to an examiner.[^10][^11] A thin build on your own rules also avoids lock-in while the NAIC vendor registry is still a draft.[^36] A common middle path: buy the reading step, and keep the rules and the decision log yourself.

pickElse: Your agency's real problem is a messy agency management system (AMS): fix that first, since juggling carrier systems is agencies' top tech challenge.[^6] Check the AI your AMS vendor already ships before adding a tool.[^43]
Your team only needs to write and summarise faster: a business plan of ChatGPT, Claude or Microsoft 365 Copilot will do. Add a one-page AI policy.[^7]
Missed calls are costing you quotes: an off-the-shelf AI receptionist such as Sonant beats a build. Sonant prices by call volume.[^46]
Simple, rules-based work such as renewal reminders: plain workflow automation, like the renewal automation in AgencyZoom, may be enough.[^27]

offer.heading: Which insurance workflow should you hand to AI first?
offer.body: In 30 minutes we map one workflow, such as submissions, claim files or policy checks. You leave knowing who signs off, the measure to track and which of your states' AI rules apply.

reviews.notes: Wants the first process to fix and a before-and-after measure. Ranked list gives both, but the 'On this page' list was out of page order and the first-job line was vague; reordered it and renamed it 'Your first AI job: carrier, MGA or agency'. MGA was undefined in the bottom line; defined it. Would distrust the lawsuit bullet if it sounded settled; reworded to 'partly survived motions to dismiss'. No sourced time-to-deploy figure exists in the research, so none is given.

Reads on a phone between meetings. Tool table cells were long; shortened product names and cells so the 4-column table fits 390px. Patra's '200 checks' read as policy checks only; changed to 'checks or comparisons' to match the vendor's pricing. Acronyms DOI, DFS and ACT appeared without expansion; spelled out. A pickElse sentence ran 26 words; split it.

Wants to know if one team or line can pilot first. Added 'Pilot one workflow on one team, with one owner and one measured number' to the stalled-pilots watch-out. Buy-or-build claim 'most companies now buy' overstated the Menlo data; changed to 'most enterprise AI is now bought: 76% of use cases'. Offer now says what you leave with: who signs off, the measure to track and which state AI rules apply.

Head of underwriting or claims asks what the examiner will ask. NAIC rule now says examiners can ask for the AI inventory, vendor contracts and testing. Would distrust an undated survey line; the bottom line now dates the auto survey (2022). The NAIC-by-line table needed its sample scope; added that surveys covered insurers with $250M+ premium or a large state share. The 'expert review' bullet overstated the bulletin; now says it lists expert review as one way to validate. Lawsuits are described as allegations throughout.

Steve gets the answer in 10 seconds: title is his question and the bottom line is five short bullets. Published tool prices answer 'what does it cost' for agencies; carrier tools are marked 'not published'. Security worry is answered in the ChatGPT FAQ and the public-chatbot watch-out. No case from a firm his size exists in the research, so none is claimed. Job-ad count stays in its own table, not the bottom line, since it pairs with no outside source honestly.
